preamble: A change from a voiced bilabial stop [b] to a voiceless velar stop [k] alters both place and voicing at once, which makes it typologically very unusual. The only well-documented case is Berawan, a group of four closely related languages in northern Sarawak, Borneo. There, pre-Berawan intervocalic *b (and *g) regularly surface as [k] in all four dialects, while word-initial *b is preserved in all but one of 46 etyma. Blust (2005) cites it as a sound change with no apparent phonetic motivation. Beguš & Dąbkowski (2024) reconstruct unattested intermediate stages (*b > *β > *ɸ > *x > k), but no Berawan dialect attests any of them, so the documented correspondence is *b > k.

examples.note: Intervocalic *b > k, while word-initial *b is retained. In all 36 pre-Berawan etyma with intervocalic *b or *g, the four Berawan dialects show a voiceless stop.
The initial *b is kept while the intervocalic one becomes k.

sources: Blust, R. (2005). Must sound change be linguistically motivated? Diachronica 22(2), 219–269. https://doi.org/10.1075/dia.22.2.02blu
Beguš, G., & Dąbkowski, M. (2024). The blurring history of intervocalic devoicing. Journal of Linguistics, 1–20. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022226724000197
